title: North Carolina Department of Revenue v. Philip Morris U.S., Inc.
description: Whether the Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) has subject matter jurisdiction over as-applied constitutional challenges to tax statutes, or if such challenges must be dismissed by the OAH and heard by the judicial branch.
plaintiff_argument: Philip Morris argued that N.C. G.S. § 105-241.17 allows the OAH to consider as-applied constitutional challenges to tax statutes, distinguishing them from facial challenges.
defendant_argument: The Department of Revenue argued that the OAH lacks subject matter jurisdiction over any constitutional challenges to tax statutes, whether facial or as-applied, and that such jurisdiction is reserved for the judicial branch.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Business Court's decision, ruling that N.C. G.S. § 105-241.17 does not grant the OAH subject matter jurisdiction over as-applied constitutional challenges to tax statutes, and therefore the OAH lacked jurisdiction over Philip Morris's petition.

title: State v. Rogers
description: Whether the good faith exception to the exclusionary rule applies to cell-site location information (CSLI) obtained by law enforcement pursuant to a court order that was later determined to be unsupported by probable cause, under both the United States and North Carolina Constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the good faith exception to the exclusionary rule should apply because Detective Wenk's reliance on the Section 2703(d) Order to obtain the CSLI data was objectively reasonable, making the evidence admissible.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the good faith exception should not apply because the officer's reliance on the order was objectively unreasonable, and therefore the CSLI data should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, concluding that the trial court correctly denied the defendant's motion to suppress because neither the United States Constitution nor the North Carolina Constitution required the exclusion of the CSLI due to the application of the good faith exception.

title: Mohebali v. Hayes
description: Whether a legislative cap on noneconomic damages in medical malpractice cases violates a plaintiff's right to a jury trial under the North Carolina Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the legislative cap on noneconomic damages is unconstitutional because it violates her right to a jury trial.
defendant_argument: The defendant, supported by amicus curiae, argued that the legislative cap is constitutional and does not violate the right to a jury trial, as the legislature has the authority to define remedies.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, concluding that the legislative cap on noneconomic damages is constitutional as applied in this case and does not violate the plaintiff's right to a jury trial.

title: State v. Kelliher
description: Whether a resentencing court, following a mandate to impose concurrent life sentences for murder convictions, retains de novo authority to determine if ancillary robbery and conspiracy sentences should run consecutively or concurrently.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Court of Appeals erred by limiting the resentencing court's discretion, asserting that N.C.G.S. § 15A-1354(a) grants trial courts de novo resentencing authority for all convictions, including ancillary ones, as long as the overall sentence complies with the previous mandate.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the resentencing court exceeded its authority under the Kelliher I mandate, which only addressed the murder convictions, and therefore lacked jurisdiction to impose consecutive sentences for the ancillary robbery and conspiracy convictions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and reinstated the resentencing court's 31 March 2023 judgments, which included consecutive sentences for robbery and conspiracy.

title: State of North Carolina v. Chambers
description: Whether a statute that allows a juror to be excused and substituted by an alternate after the jury in a criminal trial has begun to deliberate violates the state constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the statute allowing mid-deliberation juror substitution is constitutional, especially with the instruction to restart deliberations, and that the defendant waived his challenge.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the substitution of an alternate juror during deliberations violated his state constitutional right to a twelve-person jury.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that the statute allowing mid-deliberation juror substitution with instructions to restart deliberations does not violate the state constitution.

title: Howell v. Cooper; North Carolina Bar and Tavern Association v. Stein
description: Whether Governor Cooper's executive orders restricting bar operations during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the plaintiffs' constitutional rights under the Fruits of Labor and Equal Protection Clauses, and statutory rights under the Emergency Management Act and Public Records Act.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, bar owners and employees, argued that the Governor's executive orders arbitrarily restricted their businesses for over 400 days without sufficient scientific justification, violating their fundamental right to earn a living and equal protection, and statutory rights.
defendant_argument: Governor Cooper contended that the executive orders were necessary public health measures based on science and data to slow the spread of COVID-19, and that sovereign immunity precluded some of the plaintiffs' claims.
decision_outcome: The court modified and affirmed in part the Court of Appeals' decision on the Fruits of Labor claim, remanding it for further factual discovery, reversed the Court of Appeals' Equal Protection determination, and affirmed the dismissal of plaintiffs' statutory claims.

title: Happel v. Board of Education
description: Whether the federal Public Readiness and Emergency Preparedness (PREP) Act immunizes state actors from claims of battery and violations of state constitutional rights for forcibly vaccinating a child without consent, with plaintiffs arguing it does not cover unconstitutional conduct or non-tortious 'loss' and defendants arguing it provides complete immunity for all state law claims.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the PREP Act's immunity does not extend to unconstitutional conduct or to claims that are not 'for loss' as defined by the Act, asserting their state constitutional rights to parental control and bodily autonomy were violated by the forced, nonmandatory vaccination.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the PREP Act provides broad immunity from all state law claims, including battery and state constitutional violations, because it preempts any conflicting state laws and their actions fell within the scope of covered countermeasures.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the dismissal of the battery claim but reversed the dismissal of the state constitutional claims, remanding the case for further proceedings on the constitutional issues.

title: North Carolina NAACP v. Moore
description: Whether legislators elected from unconstitutionally racially gerrymandered districts possess the authority to initiate the process of changing the North Carolina Constitution by proposing constitutional amendments.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the General Assembly, being illegally composed of and tainted by usurpers elected from unconstitutionally gerrymandered districts, lacked the legitimate authority to propose constitutional amendments.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the legislators, even if elected from unconstitutionally drawn districts, remained de facto officers entitled to exercise all legislative powers, and that upholding their actions was necessary to avoid chaos and confusion.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, which had overturned the trial court's order declaring the Voter ID and Tax Cap Amendments void, and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings to determine if the amendments should be invalidated based on specific criteria.

title: Griffin v. State Board of Elections
description: Whether the North Carolina State Board of Elections properly dismissed election protests challenging votes based on incomplete voter registrations, lack of photo identification for military and overseas voters, and eligibility of "Never Residents", with the plaintiff arguing these votes are unlawful and the defendant arguing the protests lacked proper notice and probable cause.
plaintiff_argument: Griffin argued that ballots with incomplete voter registrations, those from military and overseas voters lacking photo ID, and votes from "Never Residents" were unlawful and should not be counted, and that the Board's dismissal of his protests was erroneous.
defendant_argument: The North Carolina State Board of Elections argued that Griffin's protests were properly dismissed due to inadequate notice to affected voters and failure to establish probable cause of an election law violation, and that its existing rules and statutes were correctly applied.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed the Superior Court's orders affirming the Board's dismissal of the protests and remanded the case, instructing the Board to allow a cure period for incomplete registrations and photo ID issues, and to remove votes from "Never Residents" from the final count.

title: State v. Francisco Edgar Tirado
description: Whether the Court of Appeals denied merits review of the defendant's constitutional challenge to his consecutive sentences of life imprisonment without parole under Article I, Section 27 of the North Carolina Constitution, and whether those sentences comply with State v. Kelliher.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Court of Appeals properly reviewed the defendant's constitutional challenge, that the sentences are constitutionally compliant under both state and federal law, and that the resentencing order did not run afoul of Kelliher.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Court of Appeals failed to provide merits review of his constitutional challenge under the North Carolina Constitution, which he contended offers broader protections than the Eighth Amendment, and that the Court of Appeals misapplied Jones. He conceded his sentence complied with Kelliher.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals, upholding the defendant's consecutive sentences of life imprisonment without parole.

title: In re Chastain
description: Whether a replacement judge has the constitutional authority to preside over a clerk's removal proceeding, whether removal can be based on allegations not included in the initial sworn affidavit, and whether the standard for removal is "misconduct" or "willful misconduct."
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Patricia Burnette Chastain, argued that the replacement judge lacked authority, that removal should only be based on allegations in the initial affidavit, and that her conduct did not meet the standard for removal.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Mr. Thompson, argued that the replacement judge had authority, that additional allegations could be considered, and that Chastain's conduct met the "willful misconduct" or "corruption/malpractice" standard for removal.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' decision, overruled a prior Court of Appeals' holding, and remanded the case, ruling that a replacement judge has authority, removal must be based only on allegations in the initial affidavit, and the standard for removal is "misconduct."

title: Mitchell v. University of North Carolina Board of Governors
description: Whether a state court should defer to a state agency's interpretation of its own rules and regulations, with the plaintiff arguing against deference and the defendant arguing for substantial deference.
plaintiff_argument: Dr. Mitchell argued that Winston-Salem State University failed to follow its own rules and regulations in his dismissal and that his letter containing racial slurs was protected First Amendment speech.
defendant_argument: The University of North Carolina Board of Governors argued that an agency's interpretation of its own regulations is entitled to substantial deference and that Dr. Mitchell's letter was not protected First Amendment speech.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court modified the Court of Appeals' judgment by rejecting the application of Auer deference to state agency interpretations and affirmed the judgment upholding Dr. Mitchell's termination.

title: McKinney v. Goins
description: Whether the state constitution limits the legislature's authority to revive previously expired tort claims by retroactively altering the applicable statute of limitations, and whether the expiration of a tort claim's statute of limitations creates a constitutionally protected vested right.
plaintiff_argument: The SAFE Child Act's revival window is constitutional because the expiration of a statute of limitations does not create a vested right, and the legislature has the authority to retroactively alter procedural remedies.
defendant_argument: The SAFE Child Act's revival window is unconstitutional because the expiration of a tort claim's statute of limitations creates a constitutionally protected vested right, which is immune from legislative interference.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the SAFE Child Act's provision reviving time-barred tort claims is facially constitutional because the running of a statute of limitations does not create a constitutionally protected vested right.

title: Askew v. City of Kinston
description: Whether plaintiffs bringing constitutional claims (Corum claims) must first exhaust administrative remedies before their case can be heard in court.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argue that administrative exhaustion should not be a jurisdictional prerequisite for Corum claims, especially when the administrative process cannot adequately address constitutional violations like racial discrimination or arbitrary government action.
defendant_argument: Defendant (City of Kinston) argues that plaintiffs must exhaust administrative remedies, and the Court of Appeals agreed, holding that administrative exhaustion is a jurisdictional requirement for Corum claims.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' decision, which had ruled against the plaintiffs on jurisdictional grounds, and remanded the case for a review of the merits.

title: Fearrington v. City of Greenville
description: Whether the City of Greenville's Red Light Camera Enforcement Program (RLCEP) and its funding mechanism, authorized by a Local Act and Interlocal Agreement, violate North Carolina's Fines and Forfeitures Clause (FFC) and N.C. G.S. § 115C-437 by allocating less than 90% of collected penalties to public schools.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the RLCEP's funding mechanism violated the FFC and N.C. G.S. § 115C-437 by diverting 'clear proceeds' of red light fines away from Pitt County public schools, as the Board received less than the statutorily required 90% of collected penalties.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Local Act specifically authorized the cost-sharing agreement, exempting them from the 10% cap, and that the program, by providing a revenue stream to schools that would otherwise not exist, aligns with the FFC's purpose.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the plaintiffs' taxpayer standing but reversed the Court of Appeals' decision on the FFC challenge, ruling that the Interlocal Agreement and Local Act do not plainly and clearly violate the FFC's text or purpose, and remanded for summary judgment in favor of Greenville and the Board.

title: Bouvier v. Porter
description: Whether the absolute privilege from defamation claims applies broadly to all individuals involved in election protests, or if it requires direct participation in quasi-judicial proceedings.
plaintiff_argument: The absolute privilege should be narrowly applied, only protecting statements made by direct participants (parties, counsel, witnesses) in judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings.
defendant_argument: The absolute privilege should broadly protect all individuals involved in any aspect of election protests, as the privilege belongs to the occasion of the proceeding, not the individual's role.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the absolute privilege broadly protects all individuals involved in election protests from defamation claims, and remanded the case for dismissal with prejudice.

title: Washington v. Cline
description: Whether the dismissal of criminal charges for a speedy trial violation constitutes an adequate remedy under the Corum doctrine, thereby precluding a separate civil claim for money damages against the State.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that vacating his criminal convictions for a speedy trial violation was not an adequate remedy and he should also receive money damages from the State for the constitutional violation under a Corum claim.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the dismissal of criminal charges for a speedy trial violation was an adequate remedy, and therefore, a Corum claim for money damages is not available.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that the plaintiff's Corum claim for money damages was barred because the dismissal of his criminal charges constituted an adequate alternative remedy for the speedy trial violation.

title: Holmes v. Moore
description: Whether S.B. 824, a voter identification law, violates Article I, Section 19 of the North Carolina Constitution by being enacted with discriminatory intent and producing a meaningful disparate impact along racial lines.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argue S.B. 824 violates Article I, Section 19 of the North Carolina Constitution due to discriminatory intent and its burden on the fundamental right to vote, creating disparate classes of voters, infringing on free elections, conditioning voting on property, and infringing on rights of assembly, petition, and free speech.
defendant_argument: Defendants argue S.B. 824 is constitutional, was not enacted with discriminatory intent, does not produce a meaningful disparate impact, and is one of the least restrictive voter identification laws.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's judgment and remanded the case for dismissal of the plaintiffs' claim with prejudice.

title: Community Success Initiative v. Moore
description: Whether N.C. G.S. § 13-1, which requires felons to complete their sentences, including probation, parole, or post-release supervision and financial obligations, before regaining voting rights, is unconstitutional due to racial discrimination, wealth-based classification, or violation of the Free Elections Clause.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that N.C. G.S. § 13-1 is unconstitutional because it discriminates against African Americans in intent and effect, creates an impermissible wealth-based classification, and violates the Free Elections Clause by preventing elections that accurately reflect the will of the people.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued that N.C. G.S. § 13-1 is constitutional, that the trial court misapplied the law and overlooked facts, and that the statute was not motivated by racial discrimination. They also contended that felons do not have a fundamental right to vote and the law does not create an impermissible wealth classification.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's judgment, ruling that N.C. G.S. § 13-1 is constitutional and does not violate the North Carolina Constitution.

title: Harper v. Hall
description: Whether the North Carolina Constitution prohibits partisan gerrymandering, with plaintiffs arguing it violates constitutional provisions and defendants arguing such claims are nonjusticiable political questions.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that legislative and congressional redistricting plans constituted unconstitutional partisan gerrymanders, violating the state constitution's free elections, equal protection, free speech, and freedom of assembly clauses, and engaged in racial vote dilution.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued that partisan gerrymandering claims are nonjusticiable political questions, as the state constitution assigns redistricting authority to the General Assembly, lacks judicially manageable standards for such claims, and does not explicitly prohibit partisan gerrymandering.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that partisan gerrymandering claims are nonjusticiable political questions under the North Carolina Constitution, overruling previous decisions (Harper I and Harper II) that held them justiciable, and dismissed all plaintiffs' claims with prejudice.

title: State v. Rollinson
description: Whether the Court of Appeals erred by concluding that the trial court complied with the statutory procedure for obtaining the defendant's waiver of his right to a jury trial for the status offense of habitual felon, where the defendant argues the court did not personally address him sufficiently, and the State argues the procedure was followed.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the trial court complied with N.C. G.S. § 15A-1201(d)(1) because the statutory language does not prohibit a defendant from responding through counsel regarding the waiver of a jury trial.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that to "address the defendant personally" and determine understanding of the waiver consequences, the defendant himself must respond to the trial court's address, and counsel responding on his behalf is insufficient.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, concluding that the trial court complied with the statutory procedure for obtaining the defendant's waiver of his right to a jury trial for the habitual felon offense.

title: State v. Diaz-Tomas
description: Whether a criminal defendant possesses the right to compel the district attorney to reinstate dismissed criminal charges and place them on a trial court's calendar for disposition, or if the district attorney retains exclusive discretion in such matters.
plaintiff_argument: The district attorney has exclusive and discretionary power to reinstate criminal charges, and a trial court lacks authority to compel such action.
defendant_argument: A criminal defendant has the right to compel the reinstatement of dismissed criminal charges and their placement on a trial court's calendar, and the Superior Court erred in denying his petition for writ of certiorari.
decision_outcome: The Court affirmed the lower court's decision, holding that a criminal defendant does not have the right to compel the district attorney to reinstate dismissed charges or place them on a trial court's calendar, and that a trial court lacks the authority to order such reinstatement.

title: State v. Hamer
description: Whether the trial court's initial noncompliance with statutory procedures for waiving a jury trial constituted structural error, thereby invalidating the defendant's waiver of his constitutional right to a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that despite initial procedural noncompliance, the trial court remedied the error, and the defendant knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to a jury trial without prejudice.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court's failure to follow the statutorily prescribed procedure for jury trial waiver constituted structural error, meaning he did not knowingly and voluntarily waive his right, and thus a new trial is required.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction for speeding, ruling that the trial court remedied any initial procedural error and the defendant validly waived his right to a jury trial.

title: Deminski v. State Board of Education
description: Whether an individual may bring a claim under the North Carolina Constitution for a school board's deliberate indifference to continual student harassment, with the plaintiff arguing such a claim is valid and not barred by governmental immunity, and the defendant arguing it is barred by immunity and that the right to education does not extend to an abusive environment.
plaintiff_argument: The defendant's failure to intervene in ongoing student harassment denied plaintiff-students their constitutional right to a sound basic education, as the deliberate indifference created a hostile environment where they could not learn.
defendant_argument: The constitutional claim is barred by governmental immunity, and the right to education does not extend to protecting students from an abusive classroom environment.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that governmental immunity does not bar the claim and that the plaintiff's complaint sufficiently alleges a violation of the constitutional right to a sound basic education.

title: Cheryl Lloyd Humphrey Land Inv. Co. v. Resco Products, Inc.
description: Whether statements made by defendants during public zoning hearings, even if alleged to be malicious misrepresentations, are protected petitioning activity under the First Amendment and the North Carolina Constitution, thus granting immunity from a tortious interference lawsuit.
plaintiff_argument: The defendants' intentional and malicious misrepresentations at public zoning hearings tortiously interfered with the plaintiff's prospective economic advantage, and therefore, the defendants should not be immune from liability.
defendant_argument: Their statements made during public zoning hearings were constitutionally protected petitioning activity, granting them immunity from the plaintiff's lawsuit.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the defendants' speech during public zoning hearings was protected petitioning activity under the First Amendment and the North Carolina Constitution, and thus the lawsuit should be dismissed.
